text: Victor Müller spent eleven years in Paris, studying the methods of Couture, Delacroix and Courbet. He became a follower of Courbet and helped to spread his technique in Germany. Born in Frankfurt, he had first trained at the art school there and then in Antwerp. He came home in 1858, but a public used to sentimental Düsseldorf pictures didn't understand his work. In 1866 he moved to Munich. His last picture, Faust on a Stroll, was left unfinished when he died in 1871.

Édouard Zier's first painting, Death of Cato, hung at the Paris Salon of 1874. Born in Paris, he learned from his father, the painter Victor Casimir Zier, and then from Jean-Léon Gérôme. The French State bought three of his early pictures, including Esther. Another one, Julia, won a gold medal at the 1876 Philadelphia Exposition. Even so, he is known mainly as an illustrator. He died in 1924.

Richard Bisschop trained as an engineer. At twenty-two he switched to art, following his uncle Christoffel Bisschop and his aunt Kate, who were both painters. He specialized in genre scenes, portraits and church interiors. When Johannes Bosboom died in 1891, Bisschop was allowed to paint him in his coffin and to sketch his workshop. He married the artist Suze Robertson, and their daughter Sara became a painter too. He worked in Rotterdam and The Hague, and died in 1926.

Sargent painted roughly 900 oils and more than 2,000 watercolors, plus countless sketches. He was born in Florence to American parents and trained there and in Paris. His Portrait of Madame X, shown at the Paris Salon in the 1880s, was meant to secure his place as a society painter but caused a scandal instead. The year after, he left for England. He lived most of his life in Europe and travelled as far as Montana. He died in 1925.

Jan van Eyck took his name from Maaseik, the town where records place his birth. He became court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and moved to Bruges in 1429. Philip sent him abroad on diplomatic trips, one of them to Lisbon to discuss a marriage with Isabella of Portugal. About 20 surviving paintings are confidently attributed to him, along with the Ghent Altarpiece. Ten carry his motto ALS ICH KAN, a pun on his name, often painted in Greek letters. He died in 1441.

Onderdonk went to Texas in 1878, hoping to paint portraits of rich citizens and save for a trip to Europe. He stayed thirty-eight years. Born in Maryland, he had studied at the National Academy of Design and the Art Students League in New York, with William Merritt Chase among his teachers. In San Antonio he helped start The Brass Mug Club, a group of artists who went out to paint in the Hill Country. He also founded the Van Dyck club for women painters. He is known as the Dean of Texas's Artists.

Tsuchiya Koitsu moved to Tokyo at fifteen and ended up in the house of the ukiyo-e master Kobayashi Kiyochika, where he stayed for 19 years. Early on he drew prints of the First Sino-Japanese War. A bout of pleurisy in 1905 forced him to give up lithography. At 60 he began working for the publisher Shōzaburō Watanabe, who also printed Kawase Hasui and Yoshida Hiroshi. His later prints used light effects to add emotional weight.

Jean Lemaire is nicknamed Lemaire-Poussin because he so often worked with Nicolas Poussin. He painted landscapes and classical architecture, filled with mythological figures in ancient dress. Born in Dammartin-en-Goële, he studied with Claude Vignon and then moved to Rome. He helped Poussin with the decoration of the Grande Galerie of the Louvre. Later he was made guardian of the king's paintings at the Louvre and the Tuileries. He died in Gaillon in 1659.

Frederick Kemmelmeyer was self-taught, and his work is generally classed as folk art. Nobody knows when or why he came to the United States. Census records give his birth year only as about 1755. Newspaper advertisements in Maryland show him offering drawing lessons and work as a miniature and sign painter. From 1803 he travelled as an itinerant portrait painter, and some paintings from those years show George Washington. His last known advertisement ran in 1816.

Paul Klee grew up in a musical house. His father taught music and his mother was a singer. Klee wrote at length about colour theory, and his lecture notes came out in English as the Paul Klee Notebooks. He taught at the Bauhaus alongside Kandinsky. His style drew on expressionism, cubism and surrealism, and the work has a dry humor and sometimes a childlike view of things. He was born in Switzerland in 1879 and died in 1940.

Armand Guillaumin worked in his uncle's lingerie shop while taking evening drawing lessons. At the Académie Suisse in 1861 he met Cézanne and Pissarro, and the three stayed friends for life. He took part in six of the eight Impressionist exhibitions. The critic Félix Fénéon called him a "furious colourist". Vincent van Gogh thought highly of his work and mentioned it in at least 36 letters, and Vincent's brother Theo sold some of it. Guillaumin died in 1927.

Johannes Christiaan Schotel was born in Dordrecht and made marine pictures for a living. He studied with Adriaan Meulemans, Martinus Schouman and the two van Strij brothers. His son Petrus Johannes became a painter too. Schotel was a good sailor himself. People admired the way he painted light on the sea. Pieter Scheen counted 214 paintings and about 275 drawings and watercolours by him.

Giulio Clovio was born in Grižane in Croatia and moved to Italy at eighteen. He trained in the household of Cardinal Marino Grimani and studied under Giulio Romano. For Cardinal Domenico Grimani he engraved medals and seals. By 1524 he was at the Hungarian court in Buda, painting for King Louis. Then Louis died at Mohács, and Clovio went to Rome. He died in 1578.

Jeremiah Meyer was born in Tübingen, the son of the painter Wolfgang Dietrich Majer, and came to England at fifteen. In London he decorated lockets and jewellery boxes with enamel to earn money. He took drawing lessons from George Michael Moser and studied enamel painting with Christian Friedrich Zincke. He became Painter in Miniatures to Queen Charlotte and Painter in Enamels to King George III. He was also a founder member of the Royal Academy. He died in 1789.

LaVerne Nelson Black was born in Wisconsin in 1887 and painted Native Americans. He lived in Taos, New Mexico, in the 1920s. In the 1930s he moved to Phoenix, Arizona, where he did two murals for the United States Post Office. His work is in the Denver Art Museum, the Fred Jones Jr. Museum of Art and the Smithsonian American Art Museum. He died in 1938.

Alexandre Cabanel was the son of a carpenter and began his apprenticeship at the Montpellier School of Fine Arts. With a scholarship he moved to Paris in 1839. He failed twice at the Prix de Rome, then won it in 1845 and lived at the Villa Medici until 1850. He painted historical, classical and religious subjects in the academic style. Napoleon III preferred him. Along with Gérôme and Meissonier, he counted as one of the three most successful artists of the Second Empire.

Egbert van der Poel was born in Delft, the son of a goldsmith. He joined the Guild of St Luke there in 1650 as a landscape painter. His best known paintings show the Delft gunpowder explosion of 1654 and what came after it. He and his wife were living nearby when it happened. They had a son and three daughters. He died in Rotterdam in 1664.

Dong Qichang first took the imperial civil service exam at seventeen and placed second to a cousin because his calligraphy was clumsy. So he trained until he became a noted calligrapher. He drew on Wen Zhengming and Zhao Mengfu, and passed the highest level of the exam at 35. In 1605 candidates demonstrated against him while he gave the exam, and he retired for a time. He was a painter, an art theorist and an official of the late Ming dynasty. He died in 1636.

Bernardo Bellotto was Canaletto's nephew and student, and he sometimes signed himself Bernardo Canaletto. In Germany and Poland he used the name Canaletto outright, which caused some confusion. His work is more somber in colour than his uncle's, and his clouds and shadows are closer to Dutch painting. He is best known for views of Dresden, Vienna, Turin and Warsaw. In 1742 he moved to Rome. Bellotto may have used a camera obscura for the precision of his city views.

Titian was born Tiziano Vecellio in Pieve di Cadore, near Belluno. His career was a success from the start, and his patrons went from Venice to the north Italian princes and finally the Habsburgs and the papacy. He and Giorgione are counted as founders of the Venetian school. In 1590 the painter Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo called him the sun amidst small stars. Titian painted portraits, landscape backgrounds, and mythological and religious subjects. He kept his interest in colour for his whole long life.

Albrecht De Vriendt was born in Ghent, the son of a decorative painter. His older brother Juliaan and older sister Clementine became painters too, and their father trained all three. Albrecht often worked with Juliaan on decorative projects. He painted genre scenes, history paintings and interiors, and also worked as an etcher and a copyist. Later he directed the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Antwerp. He died in Antwerp in 1900.

Kanō Tsunenobu studied first under his father Kanō Naonobu, and then under his uncle Kanō Tan'yū after his father died. He became a master painter. In 1674 he succeeded Tan'yū as head of the Kanō school. Many works credited to Tan'yū might really be Tsunenobu's, but it is hard to tell because the two often worked on large pieces together. He lived from 1636 to 1713.

Verner Thomé was born in Alajärvi, Finland, one of eight children. His first job was at a lithographic company that commissioned posters from Finnish artists. He studied at the Helsinki University Art School, and in 1898 at the Finnish League of Artists under Helene Schjerfbeck, but left because of poor health. He spent 1901 and 1902 in Munich. Vitalism, a German-Scandinavian movement, influenced his graphic work.

Hieronymus Bosch was born Jheronimus van Aken, in his grandfather's house in 's-Hertogenbosch, and spent most of his life in that town. His surname points to Aachen, where his forefathers had roots. Little is known about him, though some records survive. His oil paintings on oak mostly show fantastic versions of religious stories. Collectors in the Netherlands, Austria and Spain bought his work while he was alive, and it was widely copied, especially his nightmarish scenes of hell. He died in 1516.

Isaac Levitan was born into a poor but educated Jewish family in what is now Lithuania. The family moved to Moscow, and in 1873 he entered the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture, where his older brother Avel had studied before him. After a year in the copying class he moved to a naturalistic class, and soon to a landscape class. He pushed landscape painting toward what is called the mood landscape. He died in 1900.

Carl Gottlieb Peschel was born in Dresden and became a student at the Dresden Academy in 1812. A part of his father's military pension paid for a study trip to Rome with his friend Adolf Zimmermann. Back home he gave drawing lessons and painted snuff cans until the Saxon Art Association bought his Eliezer and Rebecca at the Well. He then took over the frescoes at the Härtel House in Leipzig after Bonaventura Genelli quarrelled and walked off the job. He belonged to the Nazarene movement.

Victor Higgins moved from Indiana to Chicago at fifteen and studied at the Art Institute and the Chicago Academy of Fine Arts. In Paris he learned from Robert Henri and René Menard. In Munich he studied with Hans von Hayek. He settled in Taos, New Mexico, in 1913 and joined the Taos Society of Artists in 1917. He sat on the founding board of the Harwood Foundation. He married Sara Parsons, and was later briefly married to Marion Koogler McNay.

Charles Verlat was born in Antwerp, the son of a soap manufacturer. His mother arranged his first drawing classes, and he left school at fourteen. He painted animals and portraits, but also Orientalist works, genre scenes and a number of singeries. Later he directed the Antwerp Academy. In 1886 Vincent van Gogh spent a short time there as a student, and the two men argued about van Gogh's unconventional drawing.

Giorgione came from Castelfranco Veneto, about 40 km inland from Venice, and died in his thirties in 1510. Little is known about his life. Most of it comes from Vasari. Only about six surviving paintings are firmly attributed to him. Nobody is sure what they mean, which has made him one of the most mysterious figures in European art. With the younger Titian, he founded the Venetian school, which is known for its use of colour and mood.

Giotto was a painter and architect from Florence who worked in the Late Middle Ages. His contemporary Giovanni Villani called him the most sovereign master of painting in his time, who drew all his figures according to nature. Vasari said he broke decisively with the Byzantine style. His masterwork is the decoration of the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, also called the Arena Chapel. He died in 1337.

Hugo Charlemont was born in Jemnice, Moravia, the son of the miniature painter Matthias Adolf Charlemont. His brothers Eduard and Theodor were painters too, and so was his daughter Lilly. From 1873 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna under Eduard von Lichtenfels. He painted landscapes, still lifes, genre subjects, animals and portraits. He died in Vienna in 1939.

Sano di Pietro was a Sienese painter, active for about half a century alongside Giovanni di Paolo and Sassetta. His name entered the roll of painters in 1428 and stayed there until he died. He ran a workshop with pupils and assistants. He twice led the San Donato district of Siena. Once, in 1475, he was called in to settle a dispute between the painters Neroccio di Bartolommeo and Francesco di Giorgio Martini.

Charles-Antoine Coypel was born in Paris into a family of successful history painters. His grandfather Noël was director of the French Academy in Rome, and his father Antoine received many commissions from the royal family. Charles-Antoine inherited his father's title of Keeper of the paintings and drawings of the king. He became court painter and director of the Académie Royale. He was also an art critic and a playwright. He died in 1752.

Fernand Khnopff was a founding member of the avant-garde group Les XX in 1883. His paintings often show isolation and desire, and his sister Marguerite appears in many of his portraits. He befriended Edward Burne-Jones and from 1895 was Brussels correspondent for the art journal The Studio. His Caress of the Sphinx influenced Gustav Klimt after Khnopff showed 21 works at the first Vienna Secession exhibition in 1898. He also designed theater sets and opera costumes.

Elisabetta Sirani died in unexplained circumstances at 27. She was one of the first women artists in early modern Bologna and made public altarpieces as well as private commissions. Her father Giovanni Andrea was a painter and a favorite assistant of Guido Reni. He took over Reni's teaching, and she first trained in his studio. She worked as a painter and printmaker in the Baroque style. She lived from 1638 to 1665.

Henry Luyten was born in Roermond in the Netherlands and became a Belgian painter. He studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp from 1878. In Paris he spent ten months at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and then returned to Antwerp. In 1884 he joined the art circle Als ik kan. He painted genre scenes, marines, landscapes, portraits and animals. He died in Brasschaat in 1945.

Xia Gui was a Chinese landscape painter of the Song dynasty, and very little is known about his life. No record survives of his birth, death or schooling. Only a few of his works remain. He continued the tradition of Li Tang and simplified the earlier Song style. With Ma Yuan he founded the Ma-Xia school. His reputation suffered after his death, but the Japanese master Sesshū kept his tradition going.

Bernini was the leading sculptor of his age and is credited with creating the Baroque style of sculpture. He was also an architect, a city planner and a painter, mostly of small oil canvases. He even wrote, directed and acted in plays. One scholar put it this way: what Shakespeare is to drama, Bernini may be to sculpture, the first pan-European sculptor whose name is at once tied to one manner and vision. He was born in 1598 and died in 1680.

Georges William Thornley was the son of a Welsh immigrant. He studied with the landscape painter Eugène Cicéri and with Edmond Yon. He is remembered for Normandy seascapes and landscapes of the French and Italian Rivieras. He also made lithographs after Corot, Pissarro, Degas and Puvis de Chavannes, and the Salon gave awards for them. His paintings were first exhibited in 1878. Thornley took up Impressionism early in his career.

Henry Keller was an American artist who led a generation of Ohio watercolor painters, known as the Cleveland School. He taught at the Cleveland School of Art and also ran a summer school at Berlin Heights, Ohio. His students there included Charles Burchfield, James Kulhanek, Paul Travis, August Biehle and Frank Wilcox. Keller was born in 1869 and died in 1949.

Marianne von Werefkin was a Russian-born painter who worked in Germany and Switzerland. Her father, of Russian nobility, made a career in the army and ended as a general in command of the Peter and Paul Fortress in Saint Petersburg. Her mother came from an old Cossack family. Werefkin is best known for her Expressionist works. She lived from 1860 to 1938.

Miyagawa Chōshun founded the Miyagawa school, and he and his pupils are among the few ukiyo-e artists who never made woodblock prints. He was born in Owari Province but spent much of his later life in Edo, where he died. He trained with artists of the Tosa and Kanō schools and with Hishikawa Moronobu, the master of early ukiyo-e. His figures have a soft, warm femininity. Richard Lane counts his coloring among the best in ukiyo-e. He died in 1753.

Francesco Montemezzano was born near Verona and seems to have been a follower, if not a pupil, of Paolo Veronese. He worked in Venice and on the mainland, mostly on sacred subjects. He completed some of the panels for the church of San Nicolò dei Mendicoli. The biographer Ridolfi wrote that he gave himself too much to the pleasures of love and to expensive objects, and that this led to an early death by poisoning. A painting of his appeared on the BBC programme Fake or Fortune? in 2015.

Carl Larsson was born in the Gamla stan district of Stockholm to very poor parents, and his childhood was not happy. He painted oils, watercolors and frescoes. Most people know him for his watercolors of idyllic family life. He thought his finest work was Midvinterblot, a large painting now in the Swedish National Museum of Fine Arts. He belonged to the Arts and Crafts movement and died in 1919.

Gerrit Dou was born in Leiden, where his father made stained glass. He studied drawing and then trained in a stained-glass workshop. At fourteen he was sent to study painting in Rembrandt's studio, and he stayed for about three years. His small, highly polished paintings are typical of the Leiden fijnschilders. He is known for trompe-l'oeil niche paintings and for candlelit night scenes with strong chiaroscuro. He died in 1675.

Jean-Étienne Liotard was born in Geneva to exiled French Huguenots. He worked in Rome, Istanbul, Paris, Vienna, London and Amsterdam. Portraits in pastel and scenes of life in Turkey are what he is best known for. He wrote a treatise on painting that argued painting should be a mirror of nature. He was also a printmaker and an art dealer. He died in 1789.

Maruyama Ōkyo was born into a farming family in Ano-o, near Kyoto. As a teenager he moved to Kyoto and apprenticed for a toy shop. He studied Chinese, Japanese and Western works of art, and his own style mixed Western naturalism with Eastern decorative design. He founded the Maruyama school of painting. Many fellow artists said his work was too slavishly devoted to natural representation, but laypeople loved it. He died in 1795.

Arent Arentsz was born and died in Amsterdam, and some called him Cabel. His works carry the monogram AA. He is known for summer and winter landscapes, mostly hunting and fishing scenes. Hendrick Avercamp influenced him, though the two are easy to tell apart. Some of his work hangs in the National Gallery in London and in the Rijksmuseum. He was buried in the Oude Kerk in 1631.

Juan Gris was born José Victoriano González-Pérez in Madrid. He studied engineering there and drew for local periodicals. He studied painting with José Moreno Carbonero for a year, and in 1905 he took the name Juan Gris. He lived and worked in France for most of his career, and his works are among the most distinctive of Cubism. His wife Lucie Belin gave birth to their son Georges in 1909.

Imao Keinen was born in Kyoto and began a wide education in Japanese art styles at the age of 12, including classical painting, printmaking and calligraphy. He received a professorship at the Kyoto School of Painting in 1880. His album Keinen Kachō Gafu, full of bird and flower designs, led to his place on the Art Committee of the imperial court. He was appointed an Imperial Household Artist in 1904. He died in 1924.

Pierre Bonnard was a founding member of Les Nabis, a Post-Impressionist group of avant-garde painters. His early work owed a lot to Paul Gauguin and to the prints of Hokusai. He painted landscapes and urban scenes, and he painted portraits and intimate domestic scenes where the backgrounds, colors and painting style usually mattered more than the subject. He also worked as an illustrator and printmaker. He was born in Fontenay-aux-Roses in 1867 and died in 1947.

Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun made her name as the portrait painter to Marie Antoinette. She mostly painted portraits, and she was elected to art academies in ten cities. European aristocrats, actors and writers were among her patrons. Her style is often placed in the aftermath of Rococo, with some Neoclassical elements. She was born in 1755. She died in 1842.

Bernhard Keil was born in Helsingør and became a pupil of the Danish painter Morten Steenwinkel. From 1642 to 1644 he studied with Rembrandt in Amsterdam. He later worked with Hendrick Uylenburgh and ran his own workshop. He travelled to Rome and stayed there until he died in 1687. He also worked in Bergamo and Venice. Jan Lievens influenced him, and he in turn influenced Antonio Cifrondi.
